examples.problem:
Given that

$$
\begin{aligned}L{\operatorname{sin}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{\omega }{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0, \\ L{\operatorname{cos}⁡\omega t} & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+{\omega }^{2}}, &  & s>0,\end{aligned}
$$

find $\mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t-4)\,\cos(9\pi t) \right\},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
examples.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a \ge 0$ and $\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}$ exists for $s > s_0,$ then

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-a)\,g(t)\big\}
= e^{-as}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+a)\big\},
\qquad \text{for} \; s > s_0,
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
\mathcal{L}\left\{ u(t -4)\,\cos(9\pi t) \right\}.
$$

Therefore, $a=4,$ and we have 

$$
\mathcal{L} \big\{u(t-4)\,g(t)\big\} = e^{-4s}\,\mathcal{L}\big\{g(t+4)\big\},
$$

where $g(t)= \cos(9\pi t).$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+4) & =cos\,(9\pi (t+4)) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡(9\pi t+36\pi ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t\operatorname{cos}⁡36\pi -\operatorname{sin}⁡9\pi t\operatorname{sin}⁡36\pi  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t\cdot 1-\operatorname{sin}⁡9\pi t\cdot 0 \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡9\pi t.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\mathcal{L} \left\{\cos(\omega t)\right\}=\dfrac{s}{s^2 + \omega^2}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+4)} & =L{\operatorname{cos}⁡(9\pi t)} \\  & =\frac{s}{{s}^{2}+81{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-4)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-4s}\,L{g(t+4)} \\  & ={e}^{-4s}\cdot \frac{s}{{s}^{2}+81{\pi }^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.problem: Given that $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ for $s>0$, find $L{u(t-8)({t}^{2}+5t-1)},$ where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.
feedback.worked_solution:
The second shifting theorem states that if $a\ge 0$ and $L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}$ exists for $s>{s}_{0},$ then

$$
L{u(t-a)\,g(t)}={e}^{-as}\,L{g(t+a)},\,\text{for}\,s>{s}_{0},
$$

where $u(t)$ is the unit step function.

In our case, we wish to find

$$
L{u(t-8)({t}^{2}+5t-1)}.
$$

Therefore, $a=8,$ and we have 

$$
L{u(t-8)\,g(t)}={e}^{-8s}\,L{g(t+8)},
$$

where $g(t)={t}^{2}+5t-1.$

Notice that

$$
\begin{aligned}g(t+8) & =(t+8)^{2}+5(t+8)-1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+16t+64\,+\,5t+40\,-\,1 \\  & ={t}^{2}+21t+103.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $L{{t}^{n}}=\frac{n!}{{s}^{n+1}}$ and $L{1}=\frac{1}{s}$ for $s>0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}L{g(t+8)} & =L{{t}^{2}+21t+103} \\  & =L{{t}^{2}}+21L{t}+103L{1} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+21\cdot \frac{1}{{s}^{2}}+103\cdot \frac{1}{s} \\  & =\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{21}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{103}{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying the second shifting theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}L{u(t-8)\,g(t)} & ={e}^{-8s}\,L{g(t+8)} \\  & ={e}^{-8s}(\frac{2}{{s}^{3}}+\frac{21}{{s}^{2}}+\frac{103}{s}).\end{aligned}
$$
